paragraphs.text: An occasion like this has its own distinction in that it is not of our arrangement. We are here, as our brother said in prayer, because the Lord has taken one from our midst, and it is because of the Lord’s own action that we are found gathered here, and we would expect the Lord to speak to us as gathered. The Lord has something in mind for us in what He has done. He has something in mind for our sister whom He has taken. Hers is a very blessed portion, to be with Christ, which Paul says “is very much better”, Philippians 1: 23. I remember a brother in this city once saying that we tend to think that being with the Lord is the next best thing to being here, but it is not so, it is “very much better”. For our sister, her life of responsibility and service and testimony is over she is with her Lord and Saviour, put to sleep through Jesus. Therefore if the Lord would speak, it would be in view of the benefit to us who are left, that the rest of our time might be filled up so as to be “agreeable to him”.

I have read this portion which speaks about “our house which is from heaven”. We are within a tabernacle now—a mortal tabernacle. It is a provisional condition. But what is in view is a house from heaven, that is what is in view for every one of us as believers. So the apostle says, “For indeed we who are in the tabernacle groan, being burdened”. Every one of us here would be a witness to the fact that we are mortal. The groaning refers to the mortal condition, the condition of

suffering and being liable to death. But he goes on to say, “yet we do not wish to be unclothed, but clothed, that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life”. When the Lord comes and raises those who are fallen asleep, what is mortal will be “swallowed up by life”.
When He comes for those of us who may be alive and remain, what is mortal will be

“swallowed up by life”; not simply overcome, but “swallowed up by life”. Paul writes in the previous epistle, “Death has been swallowed up in victory”, 1 Corinthians 15: 54. Being swallowed up is a very full idea. That is the prospect before every one of us. “Now he that has wrought us for this very thing is God”—God has wrought us in view of finality, a final condition, no longer a mortal condition, but a condition “swallowed up by life”, a condition that will go into eternity. How wonderful that is!

“Now he that has wrought us for this very thing is God, who also has given to us the earnest of the Spirit. Therefore we are always confident, and know that while present in the body we are absent from the Lord”. That is the condition in which we are, “present in the body” and

“absent from the Lord”. Our sister is “absent from the body and present with the Lord”, but the time of our being “absent from the Lord”, “present in the body”, is the time when we need to be committed. For our sister, her time of committal, of devotion, of responsibility and service of a testimonial character is over, over for ever. Our time of testimony is a comparatively short time, hence the need to be faithful.

I was thinking of Boaz in the book of Ruth. In chapter 3 he is engaged in the winnowing process, and he is viewed as having laid himself down at the end of the heap of corn; the threshing and the winnowing have taken place. The winnowing is a

refining process; the threshing is a violent, severe process, a process of beating; but the winnowing is more gentle; it is a wind process, blowing the chaff from off the wheat. We would all experience something of the threshing process; our sister has been an example of that. There was a time when she went through very severe suffering, but finally you could see the winnowing process, something more gentle taking place, in view of refinement, in view of a finished product, a finished article. That is what we could see with our sister, and that is what the Lord has in mind for every one of us. In chapter 3 of the Book of Ruth, Boaz is winnowing, and then he lays himself down “at the end of the heap of corn” (Ruth 3: 7). Now the corn has been secured; it has gone through the winnowing process; there is no more service to be rendered to the corn in that setting. The corn represents the finished product. I thought it might represent those who sleep in Jesus. In “the heap of corn” life is latent; there is tremendous potential which will yet come into activity and display, but meantime it is latent. He laid himself down “at the end of the heap of corn”.

We tend to forget the Lord’s satisfaction in taking His own to be with Himself. We think of the blessedness for the persons who are taken; we may be reluctant to think that theirs is a blessed portion, but it is nevertheless. But then, think of the satisfaction that the Lord has in having myriads with Himself. The larger part of the assembly He has with Himself secure, the finishing process having taken place, and there for His own pleasure, soon to be manifested. It says that Boaz’ “heart was merry” as he laid himself down at the end of the heap of corn; it is his own satisfaction in that process having taken place. But then Ruth comes on the scene. Ruth came into that threshing-floor. She laid herself down at the

feet of Boaz, She, said, “Spread thy skirt” (or thy ‘wing’) “over thy handmaid”. Boaz was active in relation to Ruth. In a sense, the Lord’s service regarding His own who are with Himself is complete, just as Boaz’ activity with the heap of corn was complete, but his activities are in view of Ruth. Ruth would represent ourselves here, the current position of those of us who are “present in the body” and “absent from the Lord”; the Lord is active towards each one of us.

As we read the remaining part of the third chapter of the Book of Ruth and the fourth chapter, we can see how Boaz is active in relation to final relationships known between Ruth and himself, and that is what the Lord is after in this time in which we are. While we are “present in the body” and “absent from the Lord” it is the time of the Lord’s service, and the Spirit’s service, towards every one of us in view of each one of us being a finished article for the Lord’s pleasure eternally. You can think of that heap of corn in relation to the personnel of the assembly secured; you can think of that heap as representing those who sleep from Abel onwards, myriads, millions, all that is now secured for the Lord’s own satisfaction, soon to be
“swallowed up by life”, life in manifestation for the pleasure and glory of God and for the heart of Christ.

So Paul says, “while present in the body we are absent from the Lord”. The very fact that we are “absent from the Lord” means that it is to be a time that calls for faithfulness, for testimony, for devoted committal; that is the time that we are in as “present in the body”. The body is what expresses what is inward. We were hearing last night about our being, our spirits, but the body is needed for expression. Those who have been taken to be with the Lord are in a sense unclothed; there

is not the same ability to express what there is. That is going to come. What an expression it will be when it does come! What is mortal will be “swallowed up by life”! But meantime we are present in the body, and there is meant to be an expression of something for the pleasure of God, and for the heart of Christ. “Absent from the Lord” is a time for fidelity, a time for testimony, and that is expressed in our bodies. “We walk by faith, not by sight”; that is because we are absent from the Lord. Soon we will see Him, we will actually see the Lord Jesus face to face; the time of faith will be over. Paul says that it is preferable “to be absent from the body and present with the Lord”, but soon, dear brethren, we will be present in the body and present with the Lord. We are going to have bodies of glory to express what God has wrought in each one of us. He “has wrought us for this very thing”. There is going to be the full expression in bodies of glory like that of our Lord Jesus Christ. Think of “swallowed up by life”; how glorious, how blessed and how triumphant these thoughts are! They are to energise us and strengthen us in our time of fidelity while “absent from the Lord”.

Therefore Paul says, “Wherefore also we are zealous”. There is a need, dear brethren, for being zealous, not half-hearted, not just nominal. “Wherefore also we are zealous, whether present or absent”, that is, whether we view ourselves as present in the body or absent from the Lord, which is the time we are in, “we are zealous ... to be agreeable to him”. May the Lord help us all. Our sister has had her active part in this city in testimony, in hospitality, in deaconess service; she has fulfilled her part. There is a need to fill the ranks in this city in which we are. May we all be more zealous “to be agreeable to him”, for His name’s sake.

This scripture, beloved brethren, brings before us the death of Sarah, a distinguished saint, a princess—her name means ‘princess’—the dignified, finished product of a long history with God and the ways of God, her years being mentioned, a hundred and twenty-seven years.

That prolonged period of formation and education had been completed. The place where she died, no doubt representing the conditions in which she died, is mentioned carefully, that she died “in Kirjath-Arba—that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan”. Where we read later it is said that Abraham buried Sarah “in the cave of the field at Machpelah, opposite to Mamre—that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan”. That is where, beloved brethren, her long history with God terminated, in this area in which Abraham dwelt, a man settled in relation to the purpose of God and stable in it, restful in it, and in communion in it, so that the heavenly visitors could come to him and be restful and be suitably entertained. That is the point which Sarah reached, where she would have dwelt, and where she died. It is a remarkable suggestion of spiritual completeness and moral completeness, and she dies.

How much there is in that that corresponds to this day, when we bury a sister of distinction at the end of a long history of formation with God. It says, “And Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her”. That too is today. Mourning has its place, as at Bethany in John 11. The Lord produces at a time like this with all of us the
spirit of mourning and weeping, making us tender, receptive, susceptible to His word. May we heed it, beloved. It comes to us, but as coming to us may we receive it.

What is especially affecting me is this expression, “And Abraham rose up from before his dead”. There is mourning, there must be mourning—the Lord Jesus Himself wept in the presence of death—but may there be with us all this rising up from before our dead, the sorrow in a very real sense carried forward, but something gained from the sorrow, and out of it, as the Lord is with us in it, and speaks to us in it, so that in a fresh way we rise up from before our dead. Abraham was to have a great accession of experience and substance. What impresses us as this chapter ends is that a certain new area was assured to Abraham for a possession. Twice that is stated—that this precious, most significant, area was “assured to Abraham for a possession”. That is, he got it in his grasp, in his grip, not only intelligently, but, I am sure, with profound affection, this area that relates to what has been secured as a result of Christ going into death. That, no doubt, would be the meaning of the cave; it is where He has been. Beloved, how could we face such an occasion as this were it not in the knowledge of the One who became dead and is living to the ages of ages? His going into death has secured a defined area in which all is victory and all is assurance, and in this area we bury our dead. How wonderful that is! We have been speaking of the blessed hope before us of being always with the Lord, of being present with the Lord; Christian burial is in this area, “the field”, the precious result, secured at such cost, of the dying of Jesus. There our dead are buried, buried with affection and with honour, and with profound respect, awaiting the day when all the precious treasure in that field shall be raised.

I believe that as we rise up from before our dead the Lord would cause these things to be assured to us for a possession, not only light but a possession. Our brother has been speaking of zeal. May our energies, our lives, be within this field. It speaks in verse 17 of “the field, and the cave that was in it, and all the trees that were in the field, that were in all its borders round about”. Dear brethren, let us keep within these borders. It is an area that relates to all that opens up out of death and beyond death in which we find our life together and in which our energies and zeal are to be focused and concentrated. This was assured to Abraham for a possession. He had not had it before. I think the bearing of it upon us is that, as facing death and sorrow, and the breaking of natural ties, the Lord would give us an assured possession in a deeper sense than we have ever known before of this precious realm of life in the light of resurrection and in the light of the Lord’s soon coming for us. The trees would suggest present fruitfulness, all that is seen in the saints as the product of divine workmanship.

This chapter ends, “And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field at Machpelah, opposite to Mamre—that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. And the field and the cave that was in it were assured to Abraham for a possession of a sepulchre by the sons of Heth”. Well, beloved, may this be an assured possession to us all, this precious heritage, opening up through the death of Christ and in the light of His glorious resurrection, and in the light of the purposes of God. May the Lord bless these impressions to us for His name’s sake.

articles.title: “THE GOD OF PEACE”
articles.author: R. Swan
articles.meeting: Words at the burial of Mrs, D. L. Stewart

paragraphs.text: I should just like to add a few words, dear brethren. First of all I should like to say a word about the Shepherd. I suppose it is fitting that, as Paul no doubt wrote this epistle, he could speak of the Shepherd as being “great”. The Spirit of God delights to magnify Christ. His greatness shines in this epistle. Our sister, whom we have valued and loved and have had links with, links that will go into eternity, proved the value of the “great salvation” as Paul speaks of it in this epistle (Hebrews 2: 3), “so great salvation, which, having had its commencement in being spoken of by the Lord, has been confirmed to us by those who have heard”. What a continuity, dear brethren, of the testimony in how things have been handed down as to the greatness and glory of Christ. This “so great salvation” is great because it has been procured at so great a cost, that of the blood of Christ. Our sister knew the value of that blood and she knew the Shepherd in her lifetime and, dear brethren, not only has He given His life but in His present position, in His shepherd care and in His skill, He is bringing about what is going to meet the thought of the blessed God in taking each one of us up.

Our brother has referred to the winnowing. One’s mind went to the beginning of Luke because Luke has in mind an order of things which is perfect, which is complete, fully developed. One loves to think of the winnowing; it is in the hand of Christ, “whose winnowing-fan is in his hand”, Luke 3: 17. How skilful, dear brethren, how

touching that is, and then it says, “He will thoroughly purge his threshing-floor, and will gather the wheat into his garner”. Ah, dear brethren, think of the gathering in! But the winnowing-fan is in His hand, as if divine Persons are looking at the great end, the idea of perfection. In many ways the Lord uses the threshing-floor, often testing and drastic, but the winnowing-fan is in His hand, and I am sure our sister had a sense of that. In her closing moments, who can tell how much she must have known of the Shepherd where He is now,

“the great shepherd of the sheep”, giving her the conscious inward sense of His care and compassion? Think of how the Lord in Luke’s gospel as the great Shepherd-Priest drew near to two who were despondent. It says, “Jesus himself” (not ‘the Lord’ but “Jesus”) “drawing nigh, went with them” (Luke 24: 15); it was the great Shepherd in His priestly skill in order that there might be a bringing in and that there might be nothing lost. Dear brethren, the Lord has resources and we ought to value them, that none of us should fall out of the testimony but be carried through.

So I read from this epistle just to refer to “the God of peace”. Our sister knew the God of peace. He is spoken of as the God of peace, the God of mercy, the God of love, the God of all grace. How wonderful, dear brethren, the many ways God is spoken of, the many ways He takes, but all to the end, as our brother has been saying, to bring about a perfect end, “who brought again from among the dead our Lord Jesus”. Ah, there is One, dear brethren, who has come out from among the dead; we love to think of Him in His present position, and He is still carrying on His gracious shepherd work, but ever reminding us of “the power of the blood of the eternal covenant”. Everything, dear brethren, is established incontestable and
unalterable, the testimony in the covenant of the precious blood of Christ. How great it is! Oh how that gives stability as we think of it, “the blood of the eternal covenant”.
Then he says, “perfect you in every good work to the doing of his will, doing in you what is pleasing before him through Jesus Christ; to whom be glory for the ages of ages. Amen”.

What patience, dear brethren, divine Persons have. Not only do we value the precious blood of Christ, but are sustained. Our sister put her faith in that blood and was sustained in her spirit and in her soul and in her body. These are component parts of our being; how great they are, the spirit, I suppose, being first, the greatest, the highest part of our being. This comes into Luke’s gospel too where Mary, that outstanding vessel, speaks about her spirit and her soul—“My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour”, Luke 1: 47. How, great, these component parts! As to our beloved sister, her spirit is with the Lord, is with God, as Ecclesiastes tells us, “and the spirit return unto God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12: 7); her soul she had committed many years ago; she had committed her soul “in well-doing to a faithful Creator” (1 Peter 4: 19)—and we are about to commit her body, not just to the grave, although that is true, but to the Lord, everything intact. How peaceful everything is, the God of peace, as it were, giving us a touch of peace in the midst of it all. As our brother has said, she is in His presence, she has entered into rest, but think of a day when there will be the public manifestation of all that has been wrought out and of how our sister in quietude and in restfulness of spirit has served the Lord.

I wanted to say a word from Thessalonians because this epistle contemplates our being here when the Lord comes. The apostle speaks about those who have gone, but he says, “we, the living who remain, shall be caught up together with them” (1 Thessalonians 4: 17). That is a great thing, dear brethren. Paul must have had in his day the thought that the Lord would come at any time, but “Now the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly—and your whole spirit, and soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ”.

Oh, dear brethren, everything for the believer is intact; how restful it makes us—“the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly ...” and then “your whole spirit”. How valuable our spirits are! I think the Lord Jesus in Luke’s gospel in committing His spirit to the Father intended to help us to value our spirits, and then the Spirit helps us because in Romans it says, “The Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit, that we are children of God”, (Romans 8: 16). What restful enjoyment the Spirit would give us of this holy relationship, which our sister enjoyed.

Then how valuable our bodies are as devoted to the will of God. We can be assured and restful in the midst of all the confusion around. How restful it is to think of our beloved sister, who has been with us for over thirty years in this city, and who has served the Lord and His people, as being now with Christ. The day will come when there will be a full compensation.
May we be helped, all of us, for the time we are left, for His name’s sake.

The Lord’s table in any place may be described as the fellowship of Christ’s death on the part of all christians in that place. This was actually realised at first in the early church, but is not now seen in practice. We cannot confine the idea to our fellowship, because it takes in, in scripture, all the saints in a place ...

In trying to make clear my thought I may premise by saying that I do not believe that the truth of the Lord’s table is found outside of those gathered to the Lord apart from unrighteousness. My fear is in the assumption of the table by brethren as giving to them a kind of ecclesiastical status, when morally they may be very little in the reality of what it implies. It is a truth which in the present state of the church must be apprehended abstractly, that is, in its normal character, as being the proper fellowship of all the christians in any given place. It is the fellowship of Christ’s blood and body—of His death.

In this sense the Lord’s table in its true character can never be restored, and the attempt to lay claim to it by any body of saints appears to me undesirable. I think the point now is to be morally in the fellowship of Christ’s death, I believe it is of all moment in these days to be in the sense of the ruin of the church, and to get away, not only from all unrighteousness, but from all pretension; but to get to the Lord—to follow righteousness, faith, love, peace, with those that call on the Lord out of a pure heart (2 Timothy 2: 22). I trust that this describes our fellowship, and

am sure that the nearer we are to the Lord, the more truly we shall be in the fellowship of His death, and thus really partakers of the Lord’s table. To attempt to apply 1 Corinthians 10: 16, 17 in a literal way to ourselves, would virtually put brethren in the place of the assembly. In connection with the distinctive place which those occupy who have thus got to the Lord and are following righteousness, I quite accept the idea of a company remaining to the end. It is clear that although there may be nothing ecclesiastical, yet the existence of a company is recognised in Philadelphia.
(‘Notes of Lectures’, Vol. XVII, p.22).
Note: This does not appear to be included in the New Series.

The things spoken of in these verses are most attractive to the soul— the loving-kindness of God, the shadow of His wings, the fatness of His house, and the river of His pleasures. The desire of our Saviour God is that all men should be in the present enjoyment of them. God has no pleasure in men going on in sin with all the misery it brings. He has made every provision for their blessing and happiness at immeasurable cost to Himself and to Christ. The enemy has sown in men’s minds altogether wrong thoughts about God, but He is a Saviour God; He is rich in mercy, which means simply that there is plenty of mercy for everybody.

Myriads have already found it, and every sinner who repents towards God now will be shown mercy. What glad tidings! Instead of coming in in judgment on sinful man, God has come in in mercy as we have just sung—
‘Brightly it beamed on men forlorn,
When Christ, the holy Child, was born’.

Christ took on all man’s liabilities and bore the judgment due. He suffered, He died, He was buried, He rose again, and He is now at God’s right hand, having glorified God in respect of sin, and having fully and righteously met every claim of a holy God against the sinner. Oh the efficacy of the work of Christ, and the power and value of His precious blood, the blood of the sin-offering sprinkled upon the mercy-seat! God is now exercising His rights in mercy and not all man’s wicked devices, nor all the power of Satan, can hinder God from dispensing mercy to repenting sinners.

His loving-kindness is in the heavens (Psalm 36: 5). There it is!—far beyond the power of the enemy, and God yearns to show mercy. Zacharias speaks of “the bowels of mercy of our God” (Luke 1: 78), which shows the intensity of His desire to bless men in remitting their sins; and He can do this in perfect righteousness because of the work of Christ upon the cross.

The righteousness of God is one of the outstanding features of the glad tidings, as it says here, “Thy righteousness is like the high mountains”. We delight to call attention to it, towering majestically above all man’s sin and need, and in man’s favour. That is wonderful!
“Righteousness of God” (that kind of righteousness) “by faith of Jesus Christ towards all, and upon all those who believe”, Romans 3: 22.

You have just to take your place before God like the humble penitent who smote upon his breast saying, “O God, have compassion on me, the sinner” (Luke 18: 13), and you will prove for yourself the reality of what I am saying. That man went down to his house justified, yes, justified, for God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4: 5), that is, those who have no merits of their own. Not only your sins forgiven, never to be raised with you again—“Their sins and their lawlessnesses I will never remember any more” (Hebrews 10: 17)—but justified in Christ, the Man in God’s presence, and God regarding you as though you had never committed one sin. Justified persons have peace towards God through our Lord Jesus Christ, and they happily join with David and speak appreciatively of God’s loving-kindness as “precious”.

Then there is a moral result—“So the sons of men take refuge under the shadow of thy wings”. As having been shown mercy, you come to it that you can fully trust such a God, that you will be safe and secure under His protection; so you submit to Him and to His will. God is now to be in moral sway in grace in your soul, and that is what the kingdom means. The kingdom of God is here; it is not in display, but it is in power in the Spirit; it is moral, not material; it is a sphere of security and it cannot be moved. The simple believer who confesses Jesus as Lord proves its power on his behalf in the presence of what is adverse and hostile.

The soul of Ruth must have been filled with a sense of assurance and blessing when Boaz said to her personally, “Let thy reward be full from Jehovah the God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to take refuge”, Ruth 2: 12. How sweet that must have sounded in the ears of one who describes herself as a foreigner, one who had no right or title to blessing.
Well, that is something worth knowing, is it not?—to know the Lord Jesus as your Saviour, your Redeemer, and your Protector.

Then the passage proceeds, “They shall be abundantly satisfied with the fatness of thy house”. God has a house here where He is to be known and where you will find true satisfaction and happiness. The door is open and God Himself is inviting men to come,
“Come, for already all things are ready”, Luke 14: 17. The invitation is to a great supper. Oh let our souls be attracted by the greatness and plenitude of what God has, provided for men.

There is plenty of mercy; there is plenty of room and security under the shadow of His wings; there is plenty of room and food in His house. The largeness of God’s heart is expressed in the largeness of His provision for men. We cannot read this without thinking of Luke 15.

What a reception that repenting sinner got! And many of us can speak with joy of our reception, far beyond our expectations, and certainly not what we deserved, for we had sinned against God and deserved eternal judgment. But God forgives sins and gives the Holy Spirit to those who obey Him.

When the father fell upon the neck of the son and covered him with kisses, the son would be immediately conscious of his father’s love. And so it is with us. When God gives us the Spirit, He (the Holy Spirit) sheds abroad in our hearts the love of God; He gives us the inward consciousness of God’s disposition towards us, and how blessed that is! Then there is the best robe—we are graced in Christ, the Beloved; and the ring—the token of endless love; and the sandals—we are accorded the liberty of sonship, for God would have His sons in His house in every way suited to it and in perfect liberty. And the food is not only satisfying but abundantly satisfying. In Luke 15 it is the fatted calf, that is, Christ in His moral excellence as the One who in matchless love went through death to bring to pass God’s eternal thoughts for men. There is much food for our souls in that.

Can the world offer anything like it? Never! My heart bleeds when I think of the time and money that men waste in pursuit of the temporary pleasures of sin which cannot satisfy, when the favour of God’s house stands open to them. Satan gives nothing for nothing. His prices are very steep, famine prices for poor fare, revolting stuff, as suggested in an ass’s head and dove’s dung in 2 Kings 6: 25. If you want to find a giver you must come, in the faith of your soul, to God. In the glad tidings He is offering you the greatest things, eternal blessings, without money and without price. The invitation to you is to come and take of the water of life freely.
Then we have this precious touch, “Thou wilt make them drink of the river of thy pleasures”.

When it comes to speak of this, I feel that human language is inadequate, but I do know that it is something to be experienced in the assembly. Indeed, I felt the power and blessedness of it in my soul in assembly service this morning, especially when we sang that verse in hymn 277—
‘In Thy grace Thou now hast brought us
Sharers of Thy joy to be,
And to know the blessed secret,
Of His preciousness to Thee’.

There is a whole vast scene of glory which has its centre in Christ, and which subsists for the pleasure of God, and God would bring men into the current of what He Himself find His delight in. Oh what a God! What blessedness for men! Some low place within the door might have suited us, but that would not become God. “It became him ... in bringing many sons to glory”, Hebrews 2: 10; can you think of anything more attractive than that? God has infinite pleasure in the Man Christ Jesus, and

in all that He has brought to pass. There is His pleasure in His many sons, and much, much more. So John says, “He has given to us of his Spirit”, 1 John 4: 13. That is, God shares His Spirit with us so that we can enter feelingly, affectionately, intelligently, and responsively into all that He Himself find delight in. Wonderful!

We did not read verse 9, but God is brought before us there as the Source of life—“With thee is the fountain of life”. He quickens. He imparts life to us in Christ Jesus. He is also the Source of every blessing, and the Source of all that is glorious, the Father of glory. What a range of glory belongs to the Father! Then, “In thy light shall we see light”. God enlightens us as to the greatness and glory of Christ, the Son of God; as to His purposes; as to His promises; as to His ways with believers; as to His ways on the earth, so that we are baffled by nothing that happens there, indeed, ‘heavenly light makes all things bright’. Well, dear friends, what God presents to you in His glad tidings is most attractive. Can you remain away from Him and risk the peril of a lost eternity? We plead with you, in all affection, to come, and to come now, and you will find that all that our God would give will be yours.

articles.title: “WITH ME”
articles.author: G. W. Easton
articles.meeting: Substance of word in meeting for ministry

paragraphs.text: I want to give a word of comfort to the

brethren from this expression “with me” which is in these three scriptures. I would make an application from the first scripture to the Lord being with us wherever we may be on life’s journey; the second would apply to the end of one’s life here, even though it might be in extremity, and the third opens out what awaits us.

There is so much that would distress and trouble us at the present time, whether it be world events or the difficulties, trials, and pressures of our own lives. David was in rejection when he spoke these words to Abiathar, he was being pursued by his enemies, yet he was able to say to him, “With me thou art in safe keeping”. It is still the time of the Lord’s rejection here publicly, yet in every vicissitude of life He would give us a sense of safety, as being “in safe keeping” with Him. What a Saviour He is, and what a place of safety we have with Him, though the whole world is in turmoil! This would link with our contemplation of Him on Lord’s day in John 19 and the way He went to secure us for Himself.

Then we come to the end of our lives; if the Lord does not come for us all, we shall have to pass through the experience of death. We have read the Lord’s words to the repentant malefactor, “Today shalt thou be with me in paradise”. Paradise (or Eden) means a place of delights. It is not ‘some low place within the door’, but “absent from the body and present with the Lord”, 2 Corinthians 5: 8. Surely it will be joy unspeakable—“with me”!

In John 17 we have recorded the Lord’s request, “Father, as to those whom thou hast given me, I desire that where I am they also may be with me, that they may behold my glory which thou hast given me”. What a place it will be, and what an
occupation in such nearness to behold the glory given to Him by the Father. We do not know how soon it may be.
Oh, Jesus precious Saviour
We see Thee standing there,
With mourning ones around Thee,
Their sorrow Thou would’st share.
It fills our hearts with gladness
To know, midst sorrow deep,
Thou blessed Saviour, Jesus,
Would’st with us even weep.
Thou groanedst, then assured them
If only they’d believe
God’s glory would be shown them,
Their brother they’d receive.
Then Jesus, ever humble,
Did lift His eyes on high,
To thank His loving Father
For having heard His cry.
Then loudly He commanded
The loved one to come out,
His word and presence holy
The power of death did rout.
We know that now our, loved ones
Are present with the Lord;
Such knowledge by the Spirit
Great comfort doth afford.
And thus Thine own compassion
Most blessed Lord we’d claim,
For only Thou canst give us
What takes away all pain.
Thus Lord we would be waiting
E’en here to learn Thy mind,
Patient, Thy will fulfilling,
And balm in sorrow find.
November, 1941.
‘The Believer’s Privilege’

This poem was reproduced in the April issue from a document which attributed it to Mr. J. N. Darby. We are grateful to those who have since told us that they have copies of the verses—and confirmed that they are by J.N.D. A line was missing from the latter part of our copy, making the following couplet—
With Thee by faith I walk in crowds alone,
Making to Thee my wants and wishes known.

articles.title: EXTRACTS
articles.servant: Mrs. D. L. Stewart (with Christ 20 January 1980)

paragraphs.text: Were half the people around us put into heaven, they would get out as fast as they could.

What is in heaven is not in accordance with them: nothing they, like is there, and nothing is there that they like. Not one of us naturally would find a single thing according to our mind in heaven. So that the Lord says, “Ye must be born again”.
paragraphs.source: J. N. Darby (Coll. Wrtgs. N.S. Vol. 30, p.22)

paragraphs.text: I suppose circumcision has to do with the state in which we are, the flesh—“In his flesh”, therefore. Baptism has more to do with what is outside of us, with the world. One thus disappears out of the world ... Colossians is looking on to our going into the inheritance. This chapter is crucial; it is the chapter by which adjustments take place; I gradually pass out of the world and death altogether into the wide region of life.

My own impression is that holiness is the outcome of love, it works in that way. I see that in the epistle to the Thessalonians, they were to “abound in love one toward another...to the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father”—it works in that way.

It is most important that saints should be visited (especially if there are difficulties) whenever possible. I have found my judgment wholly changed when I met brethren and conversed with them, saw them in their locality.
